migrationOutput.description: Diagnostic output from drizzle-kit (third-party tool, shown in English).

tips.migrationTimedOut: The migration tool was killed after 2 minutes. This usually means the target database is very large or in a remote region. Re-run setup against an empty database, or run `npx drizzle-kit push` manually from a shell first and then re-open this wizard.
tips.connectionTimeout: The wizard could not reach the database host. Check the hostname spelling, that the host is publicly resolvable from this server, and that the firewall / security group allows inbound traffic on the PostgreSQL port (5432 by default).
tips.tooManyConnections: The PostgreSQL server has hit its max_connections limit. Close idle clients, raise max_connections on the server, or point the wizard at a different database for the first-run migration.
tips.readOnlyTarget: The target appears to be a read-only replica or a session forced into a read-only transaction. Re-run the wizard against the primary (writable) instance and make sure default_transaction_read_only is off.
tips.scramMismatch: The client and server disagree on SCRAM channel binding. Update your PostgreSQL client/driver, or set channel_binding=disable in the connection string if your provider terminates TLS at a load balancer.
tips.insufficientPrivileges: The database user lacks CREATE privileges on the target schema. Grant ownership of the database (or the public schema) to this user, or connect as a superuser for first-time setup.
tips.roleMismatch: The role, database, or password in the connection string does not match the server. Double-check the user, database name, and password — and confirm both exist on the target PostgreSQL instance.
tips.sslRequired: The PostgreSQL server requires (or rejects) TLS. Append ?sslmode=require to your connection URL for managed providers like Neon, Supabase, or RDS — or ?sslmode=disable for a plain local server.
tips.versionTooOld: The PostgreSQL server is older than the minimum supported version (PostgreSQL 13+). Upgrade the server, or point the wizard at a newer instance.

checks.publicUrlDesc: Fetches /api/health from the configured PUBLIC_APP_URL to confirm the server is reachable at its public address. Required for webhook callbacks, email links, and external integrations.

checks.authRoundTripDesc: Sends an unauthenticated request to /api/auth/user and expects HTTP 401. Any other status indicates the session middleware or database connection is misconfigured.
checks.authRoundTripFix: HTTP 503 means the server started before the database was ready. Ensure the database is running before starting the server, then restart. HTTP 500 may indicate a SESSION_SECRET or connection issue.
checks.migrationsDesc: Counts how many database migration files have been applied and whether any pending migrations on disk have not yet run. Migrations are applied automatically on each server boot.
checks.migrationsFix: Pending migrations were found. Restart the server — the boot-time migration runner applies all pending migrations automatically. If a migration failed, see the error panel above.

overview.title: Overview
overview.intro: The User Import feature allows administrators to bulk-create multiple user accounts at once by uploading a CSV file. This is ideal for onboarding teams, migrating users from another system, or setting up accounts in batch.
overview.step1: Download the CSV template or prepare your own CSV file
overview.step2: Fill in user details (name, email, role, etc.)
overview.step3: Upload the file using drag-and-drop or the file browser
overview.step4: Preview: review each row with its validation status (valid or error)
overview.step5: Select which users to import — deselect any you want to exclude, or go back to fix your file
overview.step6: Confirm the import and share the generated default password with imported users
overview.batchLimit: You can import up to 200 users per batch. For larger imports, split your CSV into multiple files.

prepare.option1Body: Click "Download CSV Template" in the import dialog to get a pre-formatted file with all columns, sample data, and embedded instructions.
prepare.option2Body: Create a CSV file with a header row matching the required column names. The system is flexible with column naming:
prepare.skipInstructionRows: If your CSV includes instruction rows (lines starting with ##), they will be automatically skipped during parsing. You don't need to remove them.
prepare.utf8Note: Make sure your CSV is saved with UTF-8 encoding to properly handle special characters in names. Most spreadsheet applications default to this, but double-check if you see garbled characters.

tips.title: Tips & Troubleshooting
tips.missingColumnsA: Your CSV header row is missing one or more required columns. Check that your file includes: firstName, lastName, email, role, title, department, and region. Column names are flexible (e.g., "first_name" works), but must be recognizable.
tips.emailExistsA: One or more email addresses in your CSV already belong to existing users. These rows will be flagged and skipped. Remove them from your CSV or use different email addresses.
tips.duplicateInFileA: Two or more rows in your CSV share the same email address. Each email must be unique. Check for copy-paste errors or repeated rows.
tips.invalidValueA: The value doesn't match any of the allowed options. Check the Column Reference section for valid values. Matching is case-insensitive, so capitalization isn't an issue.
tips.wontUploadA: Make sure the file has a .csv extension. Other formats (Excel .xlsx, .xls) are not supported. If your data is in Excel, use "Save As" and choose CSV format.
tips.garbledA: Ensure your CSV is saved with UTF-8 encoding. In Excel, use "Save As" > "CSV UTF-8 (Comma delimited)".
tips.bp1: Start with a small test batch (5-10 users) before doing a large import
tips.bp2: Always use the CSV template to ensure correct formatting
tips.bp3: Keep a backup of your CSV file in case you need to re-import
tips.bp4: Review the preview screen carefully before clicking "Import"
tips.bp5: Record the default password immediately - it's only shown once on the results screen
tips.bp6: Update specializations promptly after import so users have the correct access

setupGuide.intro: ImpactIQ and CriteriaIQ connect in three parts. You need Admin here and App Admin in ImpactIQ. Neither app ever writes to the other.
setupGuide.effortTitle: 1. Show SE effort on project pages (this card)
setupGuide.effort1: In ImpactIQ, a Team Leader or admin opens My Settings › API Keys and creates a key with only the effort:read scope.
setupGuide.effort2: Here, enter ImpactIQ's address, paste the key and click Save. Saving checks the key with ImpactIQ first.
setupGuide.read1: Open Admin › Integrations › API Keys. Create a key with Access set to Read only, and copy it. It is shown only once.
setupGuide.read2: In ImpactIQ, open Admin › Integrations and expand Projects (POC|POV). Under CriteriaIQ connection, enter this app's address and paste the key. Click Test, then Save.
setupGuide.read3: On the same card, choose CriteriaIQ as the Primary source, or turn on Use CriteriaIQ as a secondary source when the CRM object is the primary source.
setupGuide.liveTitle: 3. Live refresh (changes reach ImpactIQ within seconds)
setupGuide.live1: In ImpactIQ, the Live refresh section appears under the CriteriaIQ connection once it is connected. Click Turn on, then copy the Endpoint URL and the Signing secret. The secret is shown only once.
setupGuide.live2: Here, open Admin › Integrations › Webhooks, click New Webhook, choose Generic HTTP and paste the endpoint URL. Open Advanced Settings and paste the secret into Signing Secret.
setupGuide.live3: Under Events, tick project.created, project.updated, project.status_changed, criteria.updated, criteria.completed and the three MAP status_changed events (phase, step, task). Run the test, then create the webhook. ImpactIQ then shows the time of the last update.
setupGuide.more: If something doesn't work: in the webhook's View History, 401 means the secret doesn't match (make a new one in ImpactIQ and paste it again) and 404 means live refresh is off in ImpactIQ. The full guide is in ImpactIQ under How to Use ImpactIQ › Connecting CriteriaIQ.

accountName.name: Account Name
accountName.short: Select the customer account tied to this project.
accountName.long: Identify the customer organization this project supports. This should align to the account associated with the opportunity, stakeholders, and overall engagement record in CriteriaIQ.

solutionName.name: Solution Name
solutionName.short: Choose our solution or solutions being validated.
solutionName.long: Define the solution scope for the project by selecting the product or product set being evaluated. This helps frame the technical use cases, supporting resources, success criteria, and ownership model for the engagement.

industry.name: Industry
industry.short: Capture the customer’s industry or market vertical.
industry.long: Select the industry the customer operates in so the project can be better aligned to business drivers, regulatory expectations, common risks, and solution-relevant use cases.

environment.name: Environment
environment.long: Document the primary environment where the solution will be evaluated, such as on-premises, hybrid, SaaS, cloud, or a platform-specific architecture. This helps shape deployment planning, assumptions, and validation requirements.

artifacts.name: Artifacts
artifacts.short: Project resources supporting project delivery and execution.
artifacts.long: Keep every project resource in one place; store, organize, and create Documents, Links, and Code/Script snippets in a centralized artifacts library.

businessProblem.name: Business Problem
businessProblem.short: Describe the customer challenge this project addresses.
businessProblem.long: Summarize the core business issue, risk, or operational gap driving the project. Focus on the customer pain that creates urgency, such as lack of visibility, manual processes, security exposure, audit pressure, or difficulty enforcing controls.
businessProblem.example: The customer lacks visibility into privileged access activity and needs to reduce risk ahead of an upcoming audit.

solutionDescription.name: Solution Description
solutionDescription.short: Explain how the proposed solution will help the customer.
solutionDescription.long: Describe how the selected solution addresses the customer’s business problem. Include the major use cases, relevant capabilities, and expected outcomes the customer should achieve if the project is successful.
solutionDescription.example: Acme Privilege Secure will provide just-in-time elevation, session controls, and privilege governance to reduce standing admin rights and improve auditability.

mutualActionPlan.name: Mutual Action Plan (MAP)
mutualActionPlan.short: Capture the shared buyer-seller roadmap for the project.
mutualActionPlan.long: A shared roadmap between your team and ours that sets out the key steps, owners and deadlines through to a decision. It keeps both sides aligned and makes progress visible to everyone.
mutualActionPlan.example: Customer to complete security review by April 10, our team to deliver the validation summary by April 14, procurement review by April 18, target decision by April 25.

customerObjective.name: Customer Objective
customerObjective.short: Capture what the customer wants to achieve.
customerObjective.long: Document the outcomes the customer expects from the project. This should reflect their desired end state, what success looks like from their perspective, and the measurable or practical goals they want validated.
customerObjective.example: Validate that the solution can identify sensitive data exposure in Microsoft 365 and reduce manual audit preparation time.

policyConsiderations.name: Policy Considerations
policyConsiderations.short: Document security, privacy, or compliance requirements.
policyConsiderations.long: Capture any policy, governance, legal, security, or compliance factors that may influence execution. This can include access restrictions, data handling rules, regulatory obligations, internal approval processes, or change management requirements.
policyConsiderations.example: No production credentials may be shared, all test data must remain in-region, and deployment changes require CAB approval. PII, GDPR, CMMC

startDate.name: Start Date
startDate.short: Set the planned kickoff date for the project.
startDate.long: Define the target date when the project is expected to begin. This serves as the baseline for scheduling milestones, resource coordination, and overall project timing.

endDate.name: End Date
endDate.short: Set the planned completion date for the project.
endDate.long: Capture the expected finish date based on the planned scope, customer availability, and execution timeline. This helps measure project pacing and supports timeline alignment across stakeholders.

primaryEngineer.name: Primary Engineer
primaryEngineer.short: Assign the lead Solutions Engineer for the project.
primaryEngineer.long: Identify the primary internal engineer responsible for technical ownership, execution coordination, customer engagement, and successful completion of the project.

specialistEngineer.name: Specialist Engineer
specialistEngineer.short: Assign the specialist supporting deep technical needs.
specialistEngineer.long: Use this field to assign a specialist internal engineer or subject matter expert who provides advanced support for a specific solution area, product capability, or technical requirement within the project.

supportingEngineers.name: Supporting Engineers
supportingEngineers.short: List additional engineers contributing to the project.
supportingEngineers.long: Add other internal engineers or contributors supporting the project through setup, troubleshooting, workshops, demos, validation steps, or customer coverage. This helps reflect the broader execution team.

customerStakeholder.name: Project Approver
customerStakeholder.short: Identify the primary customer contact or sponsor that will approve project.
customerStakeholder.long: List the main customer stakeholder responsible for alignment, decision-making, and project coordination. This person is often the business sponsor, technical lead, or day-to-day owner helping move the engagement forward.
customerStakeholder.example: Jane Smith, Director of Identity and Access Management
